title: Juan Diego (9 December)

cards: Birdsong, before sunrise, on a bare hill called Tepeyac, which today lies inside Mexico City. An Indigenous man named Juan Diego is walking past on his way to church when the singing stops him.
Then a woman's voice calls him by name, gently, the way you'd call a child. He climbs toward it and finds a Lady standing on the hill, shining.
She has an errand for him: go to the bishop and ask that a church be built right here. She has picked her messenger.

teach.b: The story is told in the Nican Mopohua, an account written in Nahuatl, Juan Diego's own language. The first surprise is how the Lady talks to him. She uses tender forms: my littlest one, my youngest child.
The Nahuatl word is noxocoyouh. Juan Diego goes to the bishop, waits, and is politely doubted. He comes back and does something very human: he asks her to send someone else.
In the account he calls himself a nobody, small, not the kind of man bishops listen to.
Please, send someone important. She refuses. She has plenty of messengers, she says, but it's him she wants.

teach.h: HE TAKES THE OTHER PATH; SHE FINDS HIM.
teach.b: Then his uncle falls gravely ill, and Juan Diego, running for a priest, takes a different path around the hill so he won't have to face her and explain. She comes down and meets him anyway.
She tells him his uncle is already well, and asks, in effect, whether he has forgotten that she is his mother and he is under her care.
Then she sends him up the hill to gather flowers, in a season when nothing should be blooming. He carries them to the bishop folded in his tilma, his cloak.
He opens it, the flowers fall, and on the cloth is the image of the Lady that pilgrims still visit at Guadalupe. Mary's own song in Luke says it plainly.
In the Douay-Rheims: "He hath put down the mighty from their seat, and hath exalted the humble." The bishop needed a sign. It came in the hands of the man who thought he didn't count.

how: Saint Juan Diego is remembered on 9 December, shortly before the feast of Our Lady of Guadalupe; pilgrims visit the basilica at Tepeyac, where the tilma is kept, especially in those days.

games.q: you're Juan Diego. your uncle is gravely ill and you're running for a priest. the Lady's hill is on the way, and you haven't delivered her sign yet. what do you do?
o: stop at the hill as before
take another path around the hill
send someone else for the priest
games.why: he went the other way round to avoid her. she came down and met him anyway, and told him his uncle was already well.

practice: Think of the people who bring things to you and are rarely noticed: the mail carrier, the delivery driver, the person who cleans the building after everyone leaves. Choose one face, and remember one thing they've carried to you.
If you pray, thank God for them by name, or by their job if you don't know the name; if you don't, simply hold them in mind with gratitude.

wordCard.voice: Juan Diego. The Indigenous man of Tepeyac who asked to be replaced by someone important, and was chosen anyway, his cloak full of flowers.

orig.note: Nahuatl, written in the Latin alphabet: my youngest child, my littlest one, as the Lady calls Juan Diego in the Nican Mopohua.
